# Hallazgos: preguntas en la card de la sesión destacada

Los hechos en los que se apoyan las decisiones. Cada uno dice de dónde sale y si se verificó en el código o lo afirma una fuente.

## Verificados en el código

Las rutas son relativas a `app/`.

- **La sesión no guarda ningún ajuste del profe además de `enabled`.** Guarda `id`, `position`, `title`, `summary`, `enabled`, `currentSlide`, `currentStep` y `deletedAt`. Fuente: `packages/database/src/schema.ts`, tabla `sessions`.
- **El profe cambia la sesión con `PATCH /admin/sessions/:id`.** El payload acepta `title`, `summary`, `enabled`, `currentSlide` y `currentStep`. Cada cambio avisa al aula. Fuentes: `packages/contract/src/sessions.ts` y `packages/core/src/sessions/sessions.ts` (`Sessions.update`).
- **`GET /sessions` le devuelve al estudiante solo `id`, `title`, `summary` y `position`.** Fuente: `packages/contract/src/sessions.ts` (`SessionSummary`).
- **La destacada se deduce, no se guarda.** Es la última sesión habilitada. Fuentes:
  - `Sessions.featured()` en `packages/core/src/sessions/sessions.ts`;
  - la web la calcula aparte en `apps/web/src/routes/_app/index.tsx`.
- **La destacada se usa en dos lugares de la API.** Fuentes:
  - `classroomOf` en `sessions.ts` deja entrar al estudiante solo al aula de la destacada;
  - `sessionUrl` en `packages/core/src/announcements/announcements.ts` arma el link del mail. Si la sesión del anuncio es la destacada, el link lleva a la home; si no, a la home con `?sesion=<id>`. Se decide al enviar.
- **Las encuestas activas del inicio salen de `GET /polls?status=active`.** La ruta devuelve las de todas las sesiones habilitadas, y la web se queda con las de la destacada. Fuentes: `Polls.listForStudent` en `packages/core/src/polls/polls.ts`, y `apps/web/src/routes/_app/index.tsx`.
- **Las preguntas se cargan aparte, con `GET /questions?sessionId=…`.** Fuente: `packages/contract/src/questions.ts`.
- **Ninguna escritura del estudiante revisa en la API que la sesión sea la destacada.**
  - Preguntas: `packages/core/src/questions/questions.ts`.
  - Manos: `packages/core/src/hands/hands.ts`.
  - Votos de encuestas: `Polls.vote` en `packages/core/src/polls/polls.ts`.

  Las tres solo revisan con `visibleSession` que la sesión esté habilitada y no borrada. Que las sesiones anteriores sean de solo lectura lo controla solo la web, con `readOnly` (`apps/web/src/features/sessions/SessionLinks.tsx`).
- **El voto de una encuesta tiene más controles.** `Polls.vote` además rechaza la encuesta que no está activa (`PollNotActive`), también al cambiar el voto, y revisa que el voto tenga la forma del tipo de encuesta (`fitsPoll`).
- **La lista, el campo y el voto de las preguntas ya son un componente reusable.** `StudentQuestions` se usa en el aula (`StudentClassroom.tsx`) y en la hoja de Preguntas del inicio (`QuestionsSheet.tsx`), y tiene un modo de solo lectura. La pestaña Preguntas del panel del profe es `AdminQuestions`, dentro de `TeacherClassroom.tsx`. La card destacada es `HighlightedSession.tsx`.
- **El estado en vivo de una sesión es este:**
  - la slide del profe (`currentSlide` y `currentStep`);
  - las encuestas activas;
  - las preguntas sin responder;
  - las manos levantadas (`raisedHands`);
  - las novedades pendientes (`changelogEntries`).

  Fuente: `packages/database/src/schema.ts`.
- **El aula no guarda nada en memoria.** Los presentes salen de las conexiones abiertas, y el aula no tiene cómo echar a nadie. Tampoco hay un estado de "seguir al profe" en el código. Fuente: `apps/api/src/classroom/aula.ts`.
- **Deshabilitar una sesión hoy hace poco.** Avisa al aula ("session") y saca la novedad `session-enabled`. No corta conexiones ni toca manos, encuestas ni slide. Fuente: `Sessions.update`.
- **Cerrar una encuesta no crea novedades.** Cambia el estado, avisa al aula ("polls") y saca su novedad `poll-opened`. Fuente: `Polls.update`.
- **No hay operaciones en lote en el core.** Manos, encuestas y preguntas se cambian de a una. El repositorio sí tiene `updateWhere` y `removeWhere`, y `HandsStore` ya expone `removeWhere`. Fuente: `packages/core/src/repository.ts`.
- **No hay un tipo de encuesta de feedback en el código.** Los tipos son `choice`, `words` y `scale`. Fuente: `schema.ts`.

## Afirmados por los docs

Las rutas son relativas a `app/docs/`.

- **"Cada card muestra el resumen, las encuestas activas, donde el estudiante vota o deja su feedback, y los links a Material, Encuestas y Preguntas, sin cantidades."** Fuente: `architecture/estados-de-encuestas-y-sesiones.md`, Inicio del estudiante.

  Esto contradice al prototipo `prototipos/inicio-responsive.html`, que muestra cantidades en los links. El prototipo de este cambio las mantiene.
- **"Una sesión anterior muestra su material, sus encuestas cerradas y sus preguntas para leer, y en ella no se pregunta ni se vota."** Fuente: el mismo archivo.
- **"En el panel del aula el profe solo activa y cierra encuestas."** Fuente: el mismo archivo, Admin de las sesiones.
- **El inicio no recibe avisos.** Se actualiza cada cinco minutos o al recargar. Fuentes: el mismo archivo y `architecture/tiempo-real-del-aula.md`.
- **El feedback de una sesión es una encuesta.** El alumno lo responde con un emoji y un comentario. Fuente: `architecture/feedback-de-sesion.md`.

  No está en el código todavía (ver arriba).
- **Los invariantes de `architecture/invariantes.md` en juego:**
  - "El backend controla siempre las reglas de negocio, aunque la pantalla ya las haya controlado."
  - "Toda acción destructiva pide confirmación."

I expanded the open items in the "Chequeo final" section of the canvas. Each item says what's missing, which decision it comes from, and what changes depending on the answer.

**Waiting on you:**
1. **Scope of decision 33.** You said "block when it's disabled", but the question was about an enabled session that stopped being featured.
   - If the block applies only to disabled sessions, the teacher can activate a poll in an enabled session that isn't featured, and nobody can vote on it (decision 14).
   - If it applies to every session that isn't featured, polls can only be activated in the featured one.
2. **The "done" check on the timeline.** The home page draws a timeline beside the list: each past session has a "done" check, and the featured one shows its number in red. Until now the featured session was always the last one, so every session in the list came before it. With the explicit mark, there can be enabled sessions after it.
   - My proposal: the check only on sessions before the featured one; the ones after it show their number with no check.
   - Alternative: remove the timeline.
3. **The confirmation when disabling the featured session.** Disabling it closes its polls and lowers its hands, and the project rule says destructive actions ask for confirmation. You didn't ask for this confirmation. Should it stay?

**Answered by reading the code:**

4. **How the classroom view loads its polls and questions.** If it already filters by session, decision 13 changes nothing there. If it loads everything and filters in the web app, the way the home page does, that has to change.

**Can wait for the design stage:**

5. **The update to the classroom view.** Today, when a session changes, the API only notifies the classroom view if the title, summary, `enabled` or slide changed. For decision 23 to send students home, the classroom view of the session that stops being featured needs an update: either a new notification or the existing "session" one.
6. **One request or two in the modal.** If enabling and featuring are separate requests and the second fails, the session ends up enabled but not featured.
7. **The list heading with no featured session.** That list is all there is then, so "Otras sesiones" ("Other sessions") has nothing to be "other" than.

The classroom already asks the API for one session. Only the home page loads active polls for every enabled session and filters them in the web.

**1. Student classroom**
- **Session choice:** `aula.tsx:15-23` calls `useSessions()` and takes `sessions.data?.at(-1)?.id` as the highlighted session. The web works this out itself, not from a route param or a dedicated API call. It keeps that id in state (`entered`), renders `<StudentClassroom sessionId={entered}>` at `aula.tsx:33`, and navigates home if the highlighted session changes or disappears.
- **Header polls:** `StudentClassroom.tsx:36` uses `usePolls({ sessionId, status: "active" })`.
- **Polls tab:** `StudentPollsTab.tsx:14-15` uses `usePolls({ sessionId, status: "active" })` and `usePolls({ sessionId, status: "closed" })`.
- **Hands:** `StudentClassroom.tsx:35` uses `useRaisedHands(sessionId)`, which calls `api.raisedHands.list({ query: { sessionId } })` (`hands/useRaisedHands.ts:13`).
- **Questions:** `StudentQuestions.tsx:17` uses `useQuestions(sessionId)`, which calls `api.questions.list({ query: { sessionId } })` (`questions/useQuestions.ts:13`).
- **Cache keys:** query keys carry `{ sessionId }` (`api/query-keys.ts`). `useClassroom(sessionId)` opens a websocket scoped to the session (`classroom-url.ts:6`) and invalidates only that session's queries.

**2. Teacher classroom**
- `sesiones.$id.tsx` passes the route param `id` as `sessionId` to `TeacherClassroom`.
- `TeacherClassroom.tsx:26` uses `useAdminRaisedHands(sessionId)`, which calls `adminRaisedHands.list({ query: { sessionId } })`.
- `AdminPanelPolls.tsx:17` uses `useAdminPolls(sessionId)`.
- `AdminQuestions` uses `useAdminQuestions(sessionId)`, which calls `adminQuestions.list({ query: { sessionId } })` (`questions/useAdminQuestions.ts:13`).
- The teacher side always passes `sessionId`.

**3. API**
- **`GET /polls`:** `sessionId` is optional (`packages/contract/src/polls.ts:111`, `Schema.optionalKey(Ulid)`). With it, the API validates that the session is visible and returns that session's polls (`packages/core/src/polls/polls.ts:141-144`). Without it, it returns polls for every enabled session (`sessions.listEnabled()`). `status` is also optional and defaults to active plus closed (`polls.ts:149`).
- **`GET /questions` and the raised-hands list:** `sessionId` is required (`contract/src/questions.ts:29`, `raised-hands.ts:31`, `Ulid`).
- **Admin lists:** `sessionId` is required on the admin poll list (`contract/src/polls.ts:129`), the admin question list (`contract/src/questions.ts:58`) and the admin raised-hands list (`contract/src/raised-hands.ts:41`).

**4. Home-page question sheet**
- `SessionLinks.tsx:44` renders `<QuestionsSheet sessionId={sessionId}>`, which renders `StudentQuestions` and calls `useQuestions(sessionId)`. That means `GET /questions?sessionId=…`, scoped to one session. `ClosedPollsSheet.tsx:13` likewise uses `usePolls({ sessionId, status: "closed" })`.

SKILL.md

---
name: "unslop"
description: "Cut AI tells from prose meant to be read as a document. Use when writing or editing documentation, READMEs, design notes, wiki entries, specs, PR descriptions or similar long-form text, and when another skill asks for a writing pass. Do not apply to code, chat replies or short answers."
---
# Unslop

Edit text to remove AI patterns.

## Process

1. Run a first round: one opus agent, every rule below, the documents in the pass.
2. Verify each finding, then rewrite. Preserve meaning, match intended tone.
3. Run a second round: a fresh agent, the rewritten documents, and the first round's applied report. It checks every applied fix is still in place and flags anything that changed back; verify and re-apply what really slipped, and the pass ends.

## How to scan

The pass is two rounds: the first finds, the second guards what the first fixed.

A fresh agent each round is the point. An agent that has seen its own last report defends the report, repeats what you rejected, and stops looking for what it missed. The second round's agent sees the first round's report on purpose. Its job is not to re-litigate the findings but to verify they survived.

The author cannot run this pass alone, whatever the rules say. Whoever wrote a sentence already decided it earns its place, and that is the judgement the rules ask for.

Agents write nothing. When the text is a draft not yet on disk, save it to a temporary file first so it does not travel through the dispatch message. When the pass covers several documents, one agent takes all of them in the same round, since a sentence that repeats what another document already says is only visible with both open.

### Prompts

The first round:

```
You are doing an editing pass. Read <the file or files>. Do not edit anything.
Do not read anything else.

Apply ONLY the rules below. Read every sentence, and at each one ask what the
reader does differently because of it. Flag the sentence when the answer is
nothing, when it is the answer an earlier sentence already gave, or when it
breaks one of the rules. Report only what one of these rules covers.

RULES:
<every rule under Patterns to detect and fix, verbatim, numbers included>

EXCLUSIONS: an adjectival participle ("the bullets that are missing", "before a
change is done") is not a passive under 29, and an adverb that changes
the truth of the sentence ("skip it silently", "usually already") stays.

OUTPUT: one line per finding, in this format:
<file>:<line> | rule <n> | "<exact quoted span>" | <proposed rewrite>
Only sentences with a finding get a line. End with a line TOTAL: <n>.
Nothing else. No preamble, no summary.
```

The second round:

```
You are verifying an editing pass. Read <the file or files> and the report
below. Do not edit anything. Do not read anything else.

For every finding in the report, check the rewritten text still carries its
fix: the pattern the finding cited is gone and the rewrite kept every fact.
Report only findings whose fix is gone or undone, in this format:
<file>:<line> | rule <n> | "<exact quoted span>"
End with a line TOTAL: <n>. Nothing else. No preamble, no summary.

REPORT:
<the applied findings from the first round, verbatim>
```

### Between rounds

Every line is a claim, not an edit. For each one, reread the span and confirm that it is an instance of the rule cited, that the rewrite keeps every fact and the tone, and that the wording it replaces is not the house form the surrounding documents already use. Drop what fails, apply the rest, then run the second round.

The second round's lines are claims too. Reread each and confirm the fix really is gone or undone before re-applying. When the pass ends, report what both rounds found and what the second round caught slipping back.

## Patterns to detect and fix

Rule numbers are stable ids that other skills cite. A removed rule leaves a gap.

### Content

3. **Superficial -ing phrases.** "highlighting...", "ensuring...", "reflecting...", "showcasing...", "fostering...". Delete or expand with real sources.
5. **Vague attributions.** "Experts believe", "Industry reports suggest", "Some critics argue". Name the source or delete.

### Language

7. **AI vocabulary.** Additionally, crucial, delve, enduring, enhance, fostering, garner, interplay, intricate, landscape (abstract), pivotal, showcase, tapestry (abstract), testament, underscore, vibrant. Replace with plain words.
8. **Fancy ways to say "is".** "serves as", "stands as", "boasts", "features". Say "is" or "has".
9. **"Not just X, but Y."** State the point directly instead.
10. **Rule of three.** Don't force ideas into groups of three. Use the natural number.
11. **Synonym cycling.** Protagonist, main character, central figure, hero all in one paragraph. Pick one, repeat it.
12. **False ranges.** "from X to Y" where X and Y aren't on a meaningful scale. List topics directly.

### Style

13. **Em dash overuse.** Avoid em dashes entirely. Use periods or commas only (no parentheses, no en dashes, no hyphen-as-dash substitutes). If a thought needs separation, end the sentence or use a comma.
14. **Colon overuse.** Colons are fine before a list or example, not as mid-sentence connectors. "If you're coming from traditional automation: instead of registering event handlers, you describe conditions" adds nothing with the colon. Rewrite to let the point stand on its own without comparison framing. "Describing when the scheduler should fire works best as plain English." Same meaning, no crutch punctuation.
15. **Boldface overuse.** Don't bold every proper noun or acronym.
16. **Inline-header lists.** The tell is a bold label and colon that restates the line: "**Performance:** Performance improved...". Convert those to prose. A bold lead-in that ends in a period, names the item, and is followed by genuinely new detail ("**Schema in TypeScript.** Tables live in one file.") is fine, not a tell. A lead-in written as a slogan, a whole claim stated as a motto ("**Shapes say what a thing is.**", "**Nothing overlaps.**"), does not name the item and falls outside that exemption. Make the lead-in the plain instruction itself: "**Draw each kind of part with its own shape.**"
17. **Title case headings.** Use sentence case.
18. **Decorative emojis.** Remove from headings and bullets.
19. **Curly quotes.** Use straight quotes.

### Communication artifacts

20. **Chatbot phrases.** "I hope this helps!", "Let me know if...", "Of course!", "Certainly!", "Found the smoking gun!" Remove.
22. **Sycophantic tone.** "Great question! You're absolutely right!" Respond directly.

### Filler

23. **Filler phrases.** "In order to" becomes "To". "Due to the fact that" becomes "Because". Delete "It is important to note that".
24. **Excessive hedging.** "could potentially possibly be argued that it might" becomes "may".
25. **Generic conclusions.** "The future looks bright." State specific plans or facts.

### Jargon

26. **Abstract metaphor nouns.** Substrate (base), wedge, wedge in (add), vector (way, method), locus, vantage, nexus, primitive as a noun, harness as a metaphor, surface as in "API surface", bedrock, scaffolding as a metaphor, modality, paradigm, gold-plating (more than the job needs), ratchet as a metaphor (the mechanism's real name, or a limit that only tightens), evacuate for moving code (move out), endgame (the last phase), north star, flywheel. These read as technical but usually have a plainer concrete word. Pick the concrete word.

### Plain speech

27. **Say what it does, not how it feels.** "the database stays close at hand", "SQL you can read", "types that follow your schema" name a feeling. The fix names the mechanism or a number: "`.toSQL()` returns the exact string sent to the database", "a column rename fails the build". Ask what the sentence tells the reader to do or know, then write that. If you can't restate it as a concrete instruction, fact, or number, cut it. One more check: if the sentence could appear unchanged in another project's docs, it says nothing about this one. Cut it.
28. **Shorten or split dense sentences.** If the reader has to backtrack to parse a sentence, break it in two or drop clauses. One idea per sentence.
29. **Active voice.** Prefer it. Catch "is/are/was/were + past participle" and name the actor: "queries are validated" becomes "the compiler validates queries", "the file is parsed by the loader" becomes "the loader parses the file". Passive is fine only when the actor is unknown or genuinely doesn't matter.
30. **Cut adverbs, or use a stronger verb.** "runs quickly" becomes "is fast" or the number, and "significantly improves" becomes the measured delta. An adverb propping up a weak verb means the verb is wrong.
31. **Prefer the plain word.** "utilize" and "leverage" become "use", "facilitate" becomes "help", "numerous" becomes "many", "in the event that" becomes "if". The fancier synonym is rarely clearer.
32. **Mannered prose.** Metaphor or flourish where a literal phrase exists: aphorisms ("wire it or delete it"), rhetorical fragments for effect, personified code ("the plan holds it"), artifacts that talk, figurative verbs ("rides along", "stands on"), stock framing phrases. "A dial worth turning" becomes "a parameter worth varying". Say what you mean. An artifact talks when a shape, label, arrow, name, type or test "says", "shows" or "tells" something to state a rule: "shapes say what a thing is" becomes "draw each module as a rectangle and each store as a cylinder". A sentence that reports what an artifact really produced ("the test shows the bug") stays. Rule 26 covers the metaphor nouns.
33. **Over-compression.** Dropped articles, verbless fragments, symbol-speak, and abbreviations that make the reader decode instead of read. "Parser rejects bad date → exit 2, no write" becomes "The parser rejects a bad date, exits with code 2, and writes nothing." Write whole sentences with their articles and verbs, and spell out arrows and abbreviations.
34. **Describing the message instead of writing it.** Some words refer to the subject. Others refer to the text itself: how many parts it has, what order they come in, that something is about to arrive, that you are about to say it. The second kind carries no information, because the thing being announced arrives in the very next words anyway. Delete it. Then confirm the deletion by checking that every fact survived. These spans sit anywhere in a sentence, not only in front of a colon. At the front: "Two things to take into account:" and "One thing worth doing now:" and "Processing X, the next step is:". Mid-sentence: "the config is fine, but there is one thing worth flagging here". Inside a clause: "I should mention that the build fails on ARM" becomes "the build fails on ARM". Trailing: "which brings us to the next point" just goes. A whole sentence can be this kind too, when its subject is the text or a part of it ("this document", "this section", "the list below") and its verb says what the text is, covers, contains or is for: an opening that states the text's purpose or scope. Delete it, and if a fact appeared only in that sentence, state the fact about the subject instead: "This section explains how the cache expires. Entries expire after an hour." becomes "Cache entries expire after an hour." Same rule for headings: name what is in the section ("Issues found", "Considerations"), do not count it or trail it ("Two things to consider", "What follows"). A count also goes stale the moment an item is added or removed.
35. **Restating what you just said.** A second pass over the same idea, in different words at the same level of detail, telling a reader who understood the first pass nothing new. "That is the thing being deleted" after already naming what to delete. "In other words", "put differently", "that is to say" followed by a paraphrase rather than a sharpening. A closing sentence that recaps the paragraph above it, or an opening sentence and a closing sentence that state the same thesis around a body that already made it. The earlier mention can be anywhere in the text, the title and the description included, so an opening that restates the heading or the description counts too. Ask what the reader can do or know after the second version that they could not after the first. If the answer is nothing, cut it. Keep a restatement only when it adds precision, gives a concrete example, or translates a term the first version assumed the reader knew. A summary that reduces a concept spread over several paragraphs to its main points also stays. 16 is one narrow instance of this, a bold lead that restates its own line.
36. **Pronoun referent overload.** The same pronoun standing for two different things in one sentence, or a relative pronoun dropped where the wrong attachment is the easier parse. "The counts alone do not show a sentence appearing twice, a unit whose text also appears inside the unit before it, or any text it says was left behind": the first "it" is the unit, the second is the tool from the sentence before, and "any text it says was left behind" dropped its "that", so "it says" reads as the verb until "was" breaks the parse. Name the referent, or restore the "that": "inside the previous unit", "any text the tool says was left behind". 28's backtrack test finds the sentence, but splitting cannot repair it: a short sentence can still make the reader resolve one word twice.
37. **Negation where a positive fits.** Double negatives ("not uncommon", "not unlike", "nothing prevents") make the reader invert twice to recover a plain fact, and "not about" framing ("the question is not about X", "this is not a matter of Y") says what something is not while leaving what it is unstated. State the fact: "not uncommon" becomes "common", "not unlike" becomes "like", "the question is not about X" becomes naming what the question is about. A single honest negative stays ("the item does not fail").
38. **Actions turned into nouns.** An event or action written as a noun phrase ("the server failing to start", "the removal of the file", "validation of the input") and then made the subject of a weak verb ("goes in the chat", "happens", "takes place", "is needed"). The reader has to unpack the noun back into who does what to what. Write the clause with its actor and its verb: "Only the server failing to start goes in the chat" becomes "When the server fails to start, tell the user in the chat", and "Validation of the input happens in the parser" becomes "The parser validates the input". A noun stays when it names something the text keeps referring to, such as a defined term ("the migration", "the release").
39. **"What" clauses that withhold the content.** A clause such as "what a thing is", "what flows", "what the arrows cannot show" or "what a system's architecture is" points at information without giving it, and the reader has to guess what belongs there. Replace the clause with the content, or with a concrete example: "label each arrow with what flows" becomes "label each arrow with the payload or action it carries", and "a question about what a system's architecture is" becomes "a question about which parts a system has and how they connect". The clause stays when the words right after it list the content.

content.text:
1:# Decisiones: preguntas en la card de la sesión destacada
2:
3:Las decisiones de la exploración, en el orden en que se tomaron, cada una con la pregunta que respondió. Las que una decisión posterior reemplazó o cambió están marcadas.
4:
9:3. **¿En qué sesiones?** Solo en la destacada. En las demás sesiones las preguntas no van en la card: se leen como hoy, sin preguntar ni votar.
12:6. **¿Las preguntas están siempre en la card?** No: el profe habilita el modo desde la sección Preguntas del panel del aula.
24:15. **¿Qué pasa al destacar otra sesión?** Se desmarcan todas las demás y se les apaga el modo de preguntas destacadas. *(La decisión 22 lo amplía.)*
30:21. **¿Las manos levantadas entran en la decisión 14?** Sí: la API rechaza levantar y bajar la mano del estudiante en una sesión que no es la destacada.
31:22. **¿Qué pasa cuando una sesión deja de ser la destacada?** Se apaga `featured_questions`, se bajan todas sus manos levantadas y se cierran todas sus encuestas activas. Pasa tanto cuando el profe le saca la marca como cuando destaca otra.
34:25. **¿Y el feedback?** Se cierra con las demás encuestas: el alumno lo manda mientras la sesión sigue destacada.
42:    Con esto queda resuelto el choque con el invariante "El backend controla siempre las reglas de negocio, aunque la pantalla ya las haya controlado".
48:30. **¿Se puede deshabilitar la destacada?** Sí. Reemplaza la decisión 16 y su parte de la 27. Al deshabilitarla deja de ser la destacada, con lo que dice la decisión 22. Como es destructiva, pide confirmación con cuántas encuestas cierra y cuántas manos baja.
49:31. **¿El modal muestra texto debajo del switch?** Solo cuando hay otra sesión destacada, para avisar qué le pasa a esa sesión.
54:33. **¿Qué puede hacer el profe en una sesión que no es la destacada?** La web y la API bloquean activar encuestas y prender `featured_questions`. Vale para toda sesión no destacada, incluidas las habilitadas que no son la destacada.
57:36. **¿Deshabilitar la destacada pide confirmación?** Sí: dice cuántas encuestas cierra y cuántas manos baja. Confirma esa parte de la decisión 30.
58:37. **¿Cómo se entera el aula de que su sesión dejó de ser la destacada?** Se reusa el aviso "session" que la API ya le manda. Cuando una sesión deja de ser la destacada, su aula recibe "session", y la web lleva al inicio a los estudiantes conectados (decisión 23).
59:38. **¿Habilitar y destacar desde el modal es un pedido o dos?** Uno solo: el modal manda un `PATCH /admin/sessions/:id` con `enabled` y `featured`. En ese mismo pedido, la API hace lo que toca a otras sesiones y modelos (decisión 27).
----
3:Los hechos en los que se apoyan las decisiones. Cada uno dice de dónde sale y si se verificó en el código o lo afirma una fuente.
10:- **El profe cambia la sesión con `PATCH /admin/sessions/:id`.** El payload acepta `title`, `summary`, `enabled`, `currentSlide` y `currentStep`. Cada cambio avisa al aula. Fuentes: `packages/contract/src/sessions.ts` y `packages/core/src/sessions/sessions.ts` (`Sessions.update`).
12:- **La destacada se deduce, no se guarda.** Es la última sesión habilitada. Fuentes:
17:  - `sessionUrl` en `packages/core/src/announcements/announcements.ts` arma el link del mail. Si la sesión del anuncio es la destacada, el link lleva a la home; si no, a la home con `?sesion=<id>`. Se decide al enviar.
19:- **Las preguntas se cargan aparte, con `GET /questions?sessionId=…`.** Fuente: `packages/contract/src/questions.ts`.
20:- **Ninguna escritura del estudiante revisa en la API que la sesión sea la destacada.**
37:- **Deshabilitar una sesión hoy hace poco.** Avisa al aula ("session") y saca la novedad `session-enabled`. No corta conexiones ni toca manos, encuestas ni slide. Fuente: `Sessions.update`.
54:- **El feedback de una sesión es una encuesta.** El alumno lo responde con un emoji y un comentario. Fuente: `architecture/feedback-de-sesion.md`.
57:- **Los invariantes de `architecture/invariantes.md` en juego:**

# Shape with canvas

`shape` and the skills it loads keep their procedure, question rules and tree rules, the Out of scope branch included.

When the user asks for a fast track, or fast track is already on in the session, load mahou:fast-track after mahou:canvas and before starting, unless it is already in context. It changes some of this skill's engagement rules.

The document is `canvas/shape.tldr.json` in the change's scratch folder. `shape.md` in the same folder keeps the tree and each branch's prose, updated whenever the canvas changes; the canvas draws from it.

## The canvas is the tree

The root goes at the top of the canvas as a title, `Problem: <one line>`. Each top-level branch is an `area` labelled `<n> <title> · <status>`, and Out of scope is always the last one.

- **Left side: the branch's leaves**, in monospace text, with the same marks as `design-tree`. The sub-branches follow as a tree under them, `├─ <n.m> <title>  <status>` with their leaves indented, and a blank line above each sub-branch.
- **Right side: the prose**, at the branch level. The branch's own prose comes first, the statement of what is settled under it. Then each sub-branch that has prose gets a heading, `<n.m> <title> · <status>`, with its prose under it. A sub-branch without prose gets no heading.
- **Prose is plain paragraphs, all of them the same width**, 1160 units.
- **Shape draws no representations.** A diagram goes on the canvas only inside a question, and is deleted with the question's card.
- When a branch's sub-branches make it much taller than the others, lay its sub-branch sections side by side under its leaves.

Lay the branches out in tree order, read down each column and then across.

The opening tree goes on the canvas as the branch areas, each one pending, with the ✓ leaves the user brought under their areas and no prose yet. When a branch settles, ask the user to approve it there.

A dropped branch or leaf folds into Out of scope as `shape` says: delete the branch's area or the leaf, and add the ✓ leaf to Out of scope.

## Questions

- **A question is a violet card**: a rectangle with violet border and fill, titled `❓ Q<n> · <title>`, then the body, which gives the situation and ends with the question. Add a diagram, drawn with tldraw shapes, when the question is about the order things happen in, who sees what, or which part of the definition a situation touches.
- **Follow-ups stay inside the base question's card**, one at a time, until the question branch closes. The card holds, top to bottom: the base question and its diagram, a summary box, one Agent note, and the current follow-up as a violet card of its own.
- **The summary box**, a solid grey rectangle labelled `Summary · Q<n> so far`, holds what the question branch has settled and the findings that bear on it. Rewrite it each round; never add a line per answer.

# Shape

Takes an idea the user has already explored and finds what its definition leaves undecided. The output is a design tree with every branch settled.

## The tree

The root is the problem in one line. Each branch is an area of the definition. One branch always exists next to the ones the problem needs: what is out of scope.

```
Problem: <one line>
├─ <area>                                                    settled
│  ✓ <decision>
├─ <area>                                                    open
│  ✓ <decision>
│  ❔ Q4 <what is undecided>
└─ Out of scope                                              settled
   ✓ <what was raised and excluded>
```

## Opening

1. Read the problem and the decisions the user brings. Build the tree from them: the root, one pending branch per area of the definition, the Out of scope branch, and a ✓ leaf under its area for every decision already made. Show it and wait for the user's corrections. Open the first branch in the reply to the approval.

2. Open one branch at a time, in order. When a branch opens, state what is already settled under it in a few lines of prose and ask the user to correct what is wrong. The reply after the confirmation asks the frontier, which is that branch's open leaves. A situation the definition does not mention follows the Scope section of `design-tree`; a deferred one goes under Out of scope.

3. When every leaf of the branch is ✓, show the whole tree and stop. Open the next branch when the user approves.

4. When the user drops a branch or leaf outright, mid-round or before it's even opened, fold it into Out of scope instead of `design-tree`'s default of removing it with no trace: a ✓ leaf reading "<name> — <what was raised and excluded>", the same format any other exclusion there already uses. This applies whether the branch had settled leaves or was still pending.

## What a question is here

Questions are about behavior: what is captured, when it is replaced, who sees it, what happens on failure. Not about endpoints, columns, functions or files. If two answers lead to the same behavior with different code, the question is implementation and is not asked.

## What this skill is not

It does not design the system, write a scope or a plan, write documentation, or touch code. It ends with the settled tree. Anything built on the tree is a separate job the user starts.

The loading skill says what the tree is about and how deep its questions go."

# Design tree

A design tree is the record of a shared understanding built one question at a time. The user reads the tree, not the transcript. The skill that loads this one says what the root is, what the branches cover and what level the questions stay at. Load superpowers:unslop when the tree starts and hold its rules in everything the session writes: leaves, the prose under each branch, questions and reports. When that skill is not installed, say so and continue.

## The tree

The root is one line. Each branch is an area of the definition. Each leaf is one decision, and leaves can group under sub-branches when an area splits into parts the user wants to reason about separately.

Leaves carry their own mark. A branch is settled only when every leaf under it is settled. A branch that has not been opened yet is pending.

```
<root>
├─ <area>                                                    settled
│  ✓ <decision>
│  ✓ <decision>
├─ <area>                                                    open
│  ├─ <part>                                                 settled
│  │  ✓ <decision>
│  └─ <part>                                                 open
│     ✓ <decision>
│     ❔ Q4 <what is undecided>
└─ <area>                                                    pending
```

When the loading skill works one branch at a time, show the whole tree once it is built. Show it again when a branch settles and the next one opens, and once more at the end. Before every other round, show the branch being worked with its leaves and the rest of the tree collapsed to its branch lines and marks. When the whole frontier is worked at once, show the whole tree before every round and once more at the end.

## Rounds

The frontier is every question whose prerequisites are settled. Ask the whole frontier in one round, then wait. A question whose answer depends on another question still open in the same round belongs to a later round. When the loading skill works one branch at a time, the frontier is that branch's open leaves.

Number questions across the whole session. Q7 in round two is the seventh question asked, not the seventh of that round.

```
❓ **Q1** - **<title>**: <body. The situation and what is undecided. No options.>

---

❓ **Q2** - **<title>**: <body>
```

Ask in plain prose, written straight into the reply. Never use a tool to ask, AskUserQuestion or any other. A tool cannot ask without options, and options are what a question must not carry.

Every question is a decision that changes the outcome if answered differently. Before asking, check that different answers lead to different outcomes, and drop the question when they would not.

State a decision the user already made, in an earlier round or before the tree existed, as a ✓ leaf, and never ask it again. The user corrects a leaf that is wrong; the corrected leaf goes back to ❔ and joins the next frontier.

Before the first round, read the files that `status.md` lists in the change's scratch folder, such as the exploration's decision log and canvas, the prototypes and the earlier trees, unless they are already in context. A decision that any of these files shows becomes a ✓ leaf, including a decision that only a prototype shows. Write on the leaf which file the decision came from. Make your questions informed on topics that are not covered so far, avoid repeating questions that were already answered in previous artifacts.

When an open decision has only one plausible answer, because it follows from decisions the tree already settled or from how the code works today, it stays a ❔ leaf in the tree like any other question, and it is asked as a proposal: the round states the answer and the decision or the behaviour it follows from, and asks the user to confirm or correct it. The leaf becomes ✓ with the answer the user confirms or gives. A decision that more than one answer could reasonably settle is asked open.

## What a question carries

A question states what is undecided and stops. It does not list the ways it could be answered. Once you write the options, the user chooses among yours instead of thinking about the problem, and the answers they would have found on their own never appear.

The body carries the context the user needs to decide, and every piece of it is required when it exists:

- What the decision is about.
- Which earlier answers bear on it, and how. If Q3 settled that the value is derived at request time, a question about where it is stored says so.
- Which other parts of the system the answer will change, whether they are already in the tree or not.
- What the loading skill's source (a ticket, a document) says about it, when it says anything.

The body carries nothing about which answers exist. Each of these proposes an answer and none belongs in a question:

- A list of candidates, however even: "on the order, on the user, or in a separate table". Reference points from outside the tree, such as what another tool does, are context and not candidates (see How a question reads).
- One candidate with a question mark. "Should we store it on the order?" proposes an answer; "where does it live?" does not.
- A default the user did not set: "by default", "typically", "usually", "the standard approach".
- A verdict: "I'd go with", "the obvious choice", "the simplest is", "probably", "it makes sense to", "we should".
- What follows from one particular answer: "if it goes on the order, every read pays for it". Naming that the answer affects reads is context; working out the effect of one answer is a candidate.
- A confirmation, "so it goes on the order?". A decision the user settled is a ✓ leaf, and one they never settled is asked open.

Before sending a round, reread every question. Check that each question's context is complete and that the question follows the unslop rules, and cut anything from the second list. If the user does not know how to answer, they will ask.

When the user asks for the options or for your opinion, give the facts and the current state that bear on the choice: what exists, what earlier decisions constrain it, what a candidate would have to satisfy. Enumerate candidates only when they ask for that, evenly, and give a verdict only when they ask for one explicitly, marked as yours.

## How a question reads

When the user has to read a question twice to parse it, they spend the round working out what it asks instead of deciding.

- The title names the thing being decided in plain words: the field, the record, the step. "What the handler does with the record's `<field>`", not "The `<thing>` the record keeps after a `<operation>`". A title built from the mechanism makes the user reconstruct what the title refers to.
- The body first says what the thing is: what the field holds, where its value comes from, why that value and the new one can differ. Then what is undecided, then why it matters.

Give the user the context they need to decide, beyond the facts. Use these when the question calls for them:

- Start from a concrete case: one input, what the system produces from it today, and what it would produce under the decision. Use the project's own data when the session has it.
- Give reference points from outside the tree: what comparable tools or libraries do with the same thing, or examples of what the answer could be about. "PostHog keeps console output inside the recording" is a reference point; "should we keep it inside the recording?" is a candidate. The question itself still offers no candidates.
- Compare a finding with the leaves the tree already settled. Say which leaves it agrees with and which it contradicts, instead of describing it on its own.
- Name what breaks or is lost, and for whom, rather than the rule that causes it.
- Say what a term means the first time the question uses it.
- Use a representation when prose makes the user hold several parts at once. Use a diagram for where something runs, in what order, or across which boundary. Use a table when findings compare several things on the same points. Use a worked example with real values. In text, diagrams are mermaid through superpowers:mermaid and tables are markdown. The loading skill names what else its medium offers.

When the user says they do not understand a question, or asks what it means, restate it with the concrete case, reference points and representations listed above, starting from what the user can see rather than from the mechanism. The restatement replaces the question's body, keeps the question's number, and stays open.

## Scope

A question is about what the definition covers. A situation the definition does not mention is a hypothetical: a value that might be missing, a step that might fail, two requests arriving at once, a feature that might come later. A checklist in the loading skill or in a type reference may name such situations. The checklist says what to look for. It does not make each item a decision to ask.

Never ask a hypothetical as a decision on its own. Ask a hypotheticals question only when you noticed a situation that would change what the branch defines. Ask it at most once per branch, as a single question that names the situations and asks which of them the user wants to consider now. Not "what happens when X and Y are missing" but "do we consider that X and Y might be missing?". Naming situations is not naming answers. The options rule forbids candidates for a decision, not the subjects a decision could be about.

Each situation the user picks becomes a ❔ leaf in the next frontier. Record each one they defer where the loading skill says, so that it is not raised again.

## Facts

Never look up a fact on your own initiative. When a question needs a fact you do not have, say inside the question that you lack that context and offer to search for it. The user decides whether the lookup happens; when it does, it goes through mahou:lookup.

When the user asks for a check, run it, then report the result before the next round's tree, labelled by the question it unblocks. A fact about a library, a tool or anything else outside the project goes to a `mahou:researcher`, with the requirements taken from the branch being worked. A fact about the project's own code or docs goes to a scout. When the result contradicts a claim the user made or a decision already settled, say so in the first sentence.

## Answers

Each answer becomes a leaf. Read the answer literally. When it approves the question instead of answering it, state the reading you took so the user can correct it.

An answer can do more than settle a leaf:

- It can open new leaves under the same branch, asked in the next frontier.
- It can reveal an area the tree does not have yet. Add a branch for it, put its open decisions under it as ❔ leaves, and ask them in the next frontier.
- It can show that a branch mixes things the user wants apart. Add a level and split the leaves under the new parts.
- It can invalidate a settled leaf. Change the mark back to ❔ and ask again with the new information.
- It can reopen a settled branch, by adding a leaf under it or widening what it covers. The branch's mark goes back to open, its settled leaves keep their ✓, and the new leaves are asked in the next frontier. There is no separate mark for a reopened branch.
- It can drop a branch or leaf outright. Remove it from the tree. Nothing takes its place by default. A loading skill that wants a trace of what was dropped says so itself.

The tree grows during the questioning.

An answer that departs from the source the work came from, such as a ticket or a document, is recorded as a decision with the departure named once.

## Merging

The user may ask to merge parts of the tree that turn out to be one decision or one area.

### Questions

Two open questions that one answer would settle become one. The merged question keeps the lower number, its title names what both decide, and its body carries the context of both. Remove the other question's leaf and do not reuse its number. The merged question's leaf records the merge, for instance "❔ Q3 <what is undecided> (Q5 merged)". A merged question that waits on a lookup waits on every lookup the two had.

### Branches

A branch whose decisions another branch already settled folds into the receiving branch. Its settled leaves that the receiving branch does not hold yet move there, its open decisions become questions there, and the receiving branch goes back to open if it was settled. The folded branch stays in the tree as one line, marked "merged into <n>", with a leaf saying where its content went. Keeping it there leaves the numbers of the other branches unchanged.

## Ending

The frontier is empty when a round of answers opens no new question. Show the final tree with every leaf marked ✓ and state that it is complete. Ask nothing. What happens after the tree is the loading skill's business.

3:summary: "Cómo la web dibuja una pantalla mientras cargan sus datos, qué muestra cuando la carga falla y cómo responde a cada acción del usuario, al instante o en espera." 11:La web dibuja cada pantalla en cuanto se abre, con las partes que no dependen del servidor, y pone un skeleton en cada parte que espera datos. Si la carga falla, una pantalla de error reemplaza la página; si el usuario no tiene sesión o perdió el acceso, la web lo lleva al login. Cada acción del usuario responde de una de dos formas: al instante, cambiando la pantalla antes de que conteste el servidor, o en espera, con su botón deshabilitado hasta la respuesta. Si falla una acción al instante, la pantalla vuelve atrás y aparece un toast; si falla una en espera, el error aparece en su formulario o modal, o en un toast cuando no tiene ninguno de los dos. 24: Cargando --> Error: falla después de los reintentos 44:La web reintenta una carga que falla dos veces. Si sigue fallando, la pantalla de error reemplaza la página entera y lleva al inicio. Es una sola pantalla para cualquier error. Un pedido que responde que el usuario no tiene sesión o perdió el acceso lleva al login, no a la pantalla de error (ver [login y acceso](login-y-acceso.md)). 56: state "Vuelve a como estaba
toast de error" as Revertida 64: state "Error en el formulario o modal,
o toast si no hay ninguno" as Fallida 85:Cerrar sesión es directa pero queda en espera, porque no cambia nada que se pueda deshacer en pantalla: la web espera la respuesta y va al login. Votar una encuesta de opción múltiple o de escala también queda en espera, como la word cloud. La opción elegida muestra un spinner hasta que responde el servidor y las demás opciones se deshabilitan. Si el voto falla, la opción vuelve a como estaba y aparece un toast. Marcar un HTML como slides sigue la revisión de las slides (ver [API de las slides](api-de-las-slides.md)). 95:Si el servidor rechaza una acción al instante o no responde, la pantalla vuelve a como estaba y aparece un toast de error. Si falla una acción en espera, el error aparece dentro de su formulario o modal, que quedan abiertos con lo que el usuario cargó. Cerrar sesión, que no tiene formulario ni modal, muestra el error en un toast. Cada acción define el texto de su toast. Cuando el anuncio de novedades sale, la web cierra su modal y muestra el toast de éxito "Anuncio enviado." (ver [novedades por mail](novedades-por-mail.md)). Una acción que recibe una respuesta de sin sesión o sin acceso lleva al login, igual que una carga. 109:### 🔔 Toast 111:Un toast es una card con un ícono, un texto y una X para cerrarlo. El de error lleva un ícono de alerta y el texto del error; el de éxito, un ícono de check y el texto de lo que salió bien. Aparece abajo a la derecha; en el celular ocupa el ancho de la pantalla menos los márgenes. Si llegan varios, se apilan: el más nuevo queda abajo y empuja a los anteriores hacia arriba. Cada toast se cierra solo a los pocos segundos, o antes con su X. 119:El error de un campo es texto rojo, sin recuadro ni ícono, justo debajo del campo al que se refiere. Es una pieza distinta del error del formulario, que aparece dentro del formulario o modal cuando falla una acción en espera. Cuando aparece, ocupa su lugar y empuja lo que sigue, creciendo en altura durante un instante; con el movimiento reducido del sistema aparece sin animación. En un formulario con varios campos, cada campo muestra su propio error. 121:[Prototipo de las piezas compartidas: el botón en espera, el toast de error y el de éxito, y la pantalla de error](../prototipos/piezas.html) --- 2:title: "Novedades por mail" 3:summary: "Cómo kurasu registra lo nuevo de cada sesión como novedades pendientes, cómo el profe elige cuáles anunciar desde el admin de la sesión y cómo la API manda el anuncio por mail a los usuarios con acceso." 7:# Novedades por mail 11:Una novedad es algo nuevo de una sesión que el profe todavía no anunció: la sesión se habilitó, se subió un material o se activó una encuesta. La API registra cada novedad después de guardar el cambio que la origina, y la saca cuando un cambio posterior la deshace. El profe ve las novedades pendientes en la pestaña Contenido del admin de la sesión, elige cuáles incluir, escribe un mensaje si quiere y manda un anuncio por mail a los usuarios con acceso. La API borra las novedades anunciadas o descartadas, y no guarda el mensaje, que va solo en el mail. 13:## 💽 Qué guarda una novedad 15:Una novedad registra algo nuevo de una sesión para que el profe lo pueda incluir en el próximo anuncio; sus campos están en el [modelo de datos](modelo-de-datos.md). La lista no es un historial: una novedad existe solo mientras está pendiente, y la API la borra definitivamente cuando el profe la anuncia, cuando la descarta o cuando un cambio la saca. 17:## ⚖️ Qué cambios crean y sacan una novedad 22: C -->|"habilitar sesión"| S1["El servicio de novedades crea 'sesión habilitada'
en esa sesión"] 25: C -->|"deshabilitar sesión, borrar material,
primera respuesta, cerrar o borrar encuesta"| R["El servicio saca la novedad
de esa entidad"] 31: F -->|"no"| OK((Novedades al día)) 32: F -->|"sí"| X(("El cambio queda
sin su novedad")) 45:Un servicio de novedades dentro de la API crea y saca las novedades. Cada pedido que hace uno de estos cambios guarda primero el cambio y después le pide al servicio que cree o saque la novedad. --- canvas decisiones.md design.md hallazgos.md learn program-design ## 1 Preguntas en la card del estudiante · settled

Cuando el profe prende las preguntas destacadas, la card de la sesión destacada muestra un panel de preguntas arriba de las encuestas activas. El estudiante hace ahí lo mismo que en el aula: ve las preguntas, vota las de los demás, agrega nuevas y borra las suyas con confirmación. El panel muestra el campo para preguntar, las tres preguntas más votadas y las del estudiante, en orden de votos. "Mostrar N preguntas más" despliega la lista completa dentro de la card, y "Mostrar menos" la vuelve a plegar. El link Preguntas sigue abajo, como el de Encuestas, y abre el modal con la lista completa.

El inicio no recibe avisos. Las preguntas de los demás aparecen cuando la web vuelve a pedir los datos, cada cinco minutos o al recargar, y las propias apenas el estudiante las manda, porque la web vuelve a pedir la lista después de cada acción.

## 2 Preguntas destacadas · settled

Las preguntas destacadas son un ajuste de la sesión, `featured_questions`. El profe lo prende y lo apaga con un switch arriba de la lista de preguntas, en la pestaña Preguntas del panel del aula. El ajuste solo cambia la card del inicio: en el aula siempre se pregunta. Solo la sesión destacada lo puede tener prendido. La web y la API no dejan prenderlo en otra sesión, y la API lo apaga cuando la sesión deja de ser la destacada, así que una sesión recién destacada lo tiene apagado.

## 3 La sesión destacada · open

La destacada pasa a ser una marca de la sesión, `featured`, que el profe pone y saca. Deja de ser la última habilitada de la lista. Hay a lo sumo una sesión destacada, y tiene que estar habilitada. El profe la marca con un switch "Destacada" en la card de Contenido de la sesión, debajo del de habilitar. La lista de sesiones del profe muestra un chip "Destacada" en la que lo es.

Al habilitar una sesión aparece un modal con un switch "Destacada", prendido por defecto. Si hay otra sesión destacada, el modal avisa que esa sesión cierra sus encuestas activas y baja sus manos. Si no hay otra, el modal no muestra ningún aviso. Habilitar y destacar desde el modal es un solo pedido.

Destacar otra sesión, sacarle la marca a la destacada y deshabilitar la destacada piden confirmación. La confirmación dice cuántas encuestas se cierran y cuántas manos se bajan. La destacada no se puede borrar, porque solo se borra una sesión deshabilitada.

El estudiante recibe la marca con la lista de sesiones, y la web deja de calcular la destacada por su cuenta. Un cambio de destacada aparece en el inicio cuando la web vuelve a pedir los datos.

### 3.1 El inicio del estudiante · settled

Con destacada, el inicio la muestra arriba y debajo la lista "Otras sesiones", con todas las demás habilitadas en el orden del profe, también las que vienen después de la destacada. En el camino de la lista, las sesiones anteriores a la destacada llevan el check de terminada, y las que vienen después no llevan check ni número. Sin destacada, el inicio muestra solo la lista, titulada "Sesiones", y nadie entra a ningún aula. El link del mail lleva a la home cuando la sesión anunciada es la destacada, y a la home con `?sesion=<id>` cuando no lo es.

## 4 Cuando una sesión deja de ser la destacada · open

Una sesión deja de ser la destacada cuando el profe le saca la marca, cuando destaca otra o cuando la deshabilita. En el mismo pedido, la API apaga sus preguntas destacadas, baja todas sus manos levantadas y cierra todas sus encuestas activas, el feedback incluido. Cada encuesta que se cierra así saca su novedad pendiente, como cualquier cierre. Las preguntas sin responder y la slide del profe quedan como están. El aula de la sesión recibe el aviso "session", y la web lleva al inicio a los estudiantes que seguían conectados. Mientras la sesión no sea la destacada, la web y la API no dejan activar encuestas en ella.

## 5 Reglas en la API · settled

En el inicio, la web pide solo las encuestas activas de la destacada. El aula ya pide solo las de su sesión. La API rechaza que el estudiante vote encuestas, pregunte, vote o borre preguntas, o levante y baje la mano en una sesión que no es la destacada. La web y la API controlan las reglas nuevas: no destacar una sesión deshabilitada, no dejar entrar a ningún aula sin destacada, y no activar encuestas ni prender las preguntas destacadas fuera de la destacada. La API hace en un solo pedido todo lo que pasa al destacar o al sacar la marca. Con estas reglas, el cambio cumple el invariante "El backend controla siempre las reglas de negocio, aunque la pantalla ya las haya controlado".

## 6 Out of scope · settled

El tiempo real en el inicio se planteó y quedó afuera: alcanza con la actualización de hoy. Cortar desde el servidor las conexiones al aula también: el aula no tiene cómo, y la web lleva al inicio a los conectados.

## Preguntas abiertas

**Q1 · Cuál es la destacada cuando el cambio llega a producción.** Hoy la destacada es la última sesión habilitada de la lista, y el código la calcula. Con el cambio, la destacada es la sesión que tiene la marca, y cuando el cambio llega a producción ninguna sesión la tiene todavía. Sin destacada, el inicio muestra solo la lista "Sesiones", ninguna card muestra preguntas ni encuestas activas, y nadie entra a ningún aula (D17, D27). El cambio puede llegar a producción en medio del curso, con una sesión en curso. ¿Qué sesión es la destacada en ese momento?

**Q2 · Si destacar una sesión o prender sus preguntas destacadas deja una novedad para el anuncio.** Una novedad es algo nuevo de una sesión que el profe todavía no anunció por mail. Hoy hay tres: la sesión se habilitó, se subió un material y se abrió una encuesta. El profe las elige en la pestaña Contenido y las manda en un anuncio. Habilitar una sesión desde el modal ya deja su novedad "Sesión habilitada", y el link del mail lleva a la destacada según la marca (D19). Destacar una sesión y prender sus preguntas destacadas son cambios que el estudiante ve en su inicio. Cuando una sesión deja de ser la destacada, las encuestas que se cierran sacan su novedad pendiente. ¿Destacar una sesión o prender sus preguntas destacadas dejan una novedad pendiente?

**Q3 · Qué hace el profe en la pestaña Aula de una sesión que no es la destacada.** Hoy la pestaña Aula del admin de una sesión muestra la slide grande y un panel con las encuestas, las preguntas y los presentes. Ahí el profe mueve la slide, activa y cierra encuestas, marca preguntas como respondidas y baja manos. En una sesión que no es la destacada, ningún estudiante puede entrar al aula, y la web y la API no dejan activar encuestas ni prender las preguntas destacadas (D33). Las manos ya están bajas (D22). ¿Qué ve y qué puede hacer el profe en la pestaña Aula de una sesión que no es la destacada?

- **Q3 · What the teacher sees and can do in the classroom tab of a session that isn't featured.** No student can enter it, polls can't be activated, and featured questions can't be turned on.

# Design with canvas

`design` and the skills it loads keep their procedure, branch types, question rules and tree rules.

When the user asks for a fast track, or fast track is already on in the session, load mahou:fast-track after mahou:canvas and before starting, unless it is already in context. It changes some of this skill's engagement rules.

The document is `canvas/design.tldr.json` in the change's scratch folder. `design.md` in the same folder keeps the tree, each branch's prose and its mermaid diagrams, updated whenever the canvas changes; the canvas draws from it.

## The canvas is the tree

Each top-level branch is an `area` labelled `<n> <title> · <status>`.

- **Left side: the branch's leaves**, in monospace text, with the same marks as `design-tree`. The sub-branches follow as a tree under them, `├─ <n.m> <title>  <status>` with their leaves indented, and a blank line above each sub-branch.
- **Right side: the write-up**, at the branch level. The branch's own representation and prose come first. Then each sub-branch that has a representation or prose gets a heading, `<n.m> <title> · <status>`, with its diagrams and its prose under it. A sub-branch with neither gets no heading.
- **Use `design`'s types for the representations.** While a branch is open, draw its diagrams with tldraw shapes, which are easier to change as answers come in. Once the branch settles, replace each diagram with a `mermaid` shape that holds the source the final document uses. Size the shape to the diagram's own proportions, at one canvas unit per diagram unit. When the shape is wider than the branch's right side, widen every area in that column until the shape fits, so the column keeps one width. Draw a screen as a mockup copied from its prototype.
- **Prose is plain paragraphs, all of them the same width**, 1160 units, under the representation they describe.
- When a branch's sub-branches make it much taller than the others, lay its sub-branch sections side by side under its leaves.
- **A folded branch keeps its area**, labelled `<n> <title> · merged into <m>`, holding only the leaf that says where its content went.

For a branch whose type has a canvas reference under `references/types/`, read both the type in `design` and the canvas reference: draw the canvas as the canvas reference describes, and write `design.md` and the final documentation in the type's own form. A type with no canvas reference is drawn in its own form. Each canvas reference has the same file name as the type it adapts.

| The branch is about | `design` type | Canvas reference |
|---|---|---|
| What a component agrees with the rest of the system | `contract.md` | `references/types/contract.md` |
| How a value moves between components | `data-flow.md` | `references/types/data-flow.md` |

Lay the branches out in tree order, read down each column and then across.

The opening tree goes on the canvas as the branch areas, each one pending, with no leaves yet. Above the areas, an Agent note says in one line per branch what that branch settles. A branch's opening statement goes on the canvas as its leaves and its prose. The exploration, the shape tree or earlier branches may already show how part of the branch looks. When they do, and a diagram would make that part easier to follow, draw it with tldraw shapes above the prose, in the diagram form of the branch's type, and mark on it the parts that are still undecided, so the unknowns are obvious. When they do not, the opening has leaves and prose only. When a branch settles, draw its representation and prose in its section and ask the user to approve it there.

## Questions

Questions go in the open branch, on its right side, under its write-up. The branch's Agent note goes under the questions.

- **A question is a violet card**: a rectangle with violet border and fill, titled `❓ Q<n> · <title>`, then the body, which gives the situation and ends with the question.
- **Add a diagram, a table or a mockup to the card when text is not enough.** The canvas offers tldraw shapes for a diagram drawn by hand, a monospace text for a table, a mockup, and a `mermaid` shape. For example: a diagram of a library's format or of how its parts call each other, next to what the tree settled about it; a table in the summary box when findings compare options, one column per option and one row per point that matters for the decision; a small timeline with real values when the question is about order.
- **Follow-ups stay inside the base question's card**, one at a time, until the question branch closes. The card holds, top to bottom: the base question and its diagram, a summary box, one Agent note, and the current follow-up as a violet card of its own.
- **The summary box**, a solid grey rectangle labelled `Summary · Q<n> so far`, holds what the question branch has settled and the findings that bear on it. Rewrite it each round; never add a line per answer.
- **When the question branch closes**, delete the card, update the branch's leaves on the left, and update its write-up.
- **Keep two questions open for the user to answer.** A question waiting on a spike, a prototype or a lookup does not count toward the two, so there are three while one waits. Open the next question from the frontier as soon as one closes.
- **A merged question is one card.** Retitle the lower-numbered card, fold the other card's summary into its summary box, and delete the other card.

## Messages from the agent

Everything you would say in the chat goes on the canvas: how you read an answer, research and spike results, status, and requests to approve a branch. Write it as an Agent note: a grey dashed rectangle labelled `Agent`, in the branch or the question it is about. Keep one Agent note per place and replace its text each round. When a branch is done, delete its note.

## Recording

When the tree is complete, stop the canvas and continue with `design`'s Recording section in the chat.

# Design

Takes a definition the user has settled and designs the system that satisfies it: what is stored, how it moves, what rules apply, and whatever else the change needs. The level is system design. How the design lands in the code, from the package layout to the call paths, interfaces and files, belongs to mahou:program-design, which states it as representations and never as code. The test cases and manual validations that prove the design belong to mahou:test-design. The output is a settled design tree, each branch carrying its prose and its representation, handed to mahou:write-documentation to be recorded.

## Opening

1. Read the settled shape tree. Do not read code unless the user asks a question that needs it; when they do, a `mahou:code-scout` keeps the reading out of the conversation.

2. List what has to be designed, as the tree. The root is "System design", each item is a pending branch, and each item names what must be specified, not how. Order the branches from abstract to concrete so each one builds on the previous, typically data model, then how data moves, then the rules that produce it, then whatever the change adds on top. Do not propose representations yet. When the change contains several independent pieces, for instance two APIs or two features designed in one session, each piece is its own root with its own areas, worked one root at a time.

```
System design
├─ 1 <area>                                                            pending
├─ 2 <area>                                                            pending
└─ 3 <area>                                                            pending
```

3. Wait for the user's corrections. Drop items that are implementation (a migration, a schema field list, a function), or move them into the item they serve. Absorb items about prior artifacts (an earlier branch, a superseded document) into the design rather than naming them. Defer verification to after the program is designed. Open the first branch in the reply to the approval.

## Working a branch

Open one branch at a time, in order. The first opens with the tree's approval. Each later one opens when the user approves the previous branch's rendering.

1. **Pick the type.** Check `references/types/` for a reference matching the branch (see Types). Match on what the branch settles, not on the words in its title. A branch that adds or alters no entity or field is not a data model, even when it is about where a value is stored. Deciding which component persists a value into storage that already exists is a data flow. A reference says how the branch is usually split, what it needs to question and which representation has worked. It is a guide, not a rule. When the case needs a different split, different questions, another format or another diagram, work that out with the user. When no reference matches, propose a split in the opening statement and let the corrections settle it.

2. **State the branch as settled so far.** Every decision that explore, the shape tree or an earlier branch already made about this branch goes in as a ✓ leaf, and the prose under the branch states those decisions in simple terms. The prose stands on its own: no references to the current implementation, no comparison with how things work today, no mention of prior artifacts, nothing that belongs to another branch. It may say what the thing is for, not the flows that use it. Ask the user to correct what is wrong and stop. A corrected leaf goes back to ❔.

3. **Ask the frontier.** It goes in the reply after the confirmation. The reference lists what the branch needs to question; what is still open among those becomes the frontier. A situation the definition does not mention is a hypothetical and follows the Scope section of `design-tree`: raised in one question, opened only when the user picks it. Record a deferred situation as a ✓ leaf under the branch, reading "not considered: <situation>". Do not ask about the representation.

4. **Split when asked.** When the user wants the parts of a branch reasoned about separately, add a level, one sub-branch per part, and work them one at a time, each with its own prose, frontier and representation. When the parts describe one thing, the user may ask for them to render as one representation and one section once the user has settled them all; the sub-branches keep their own leaves in the tree.

5. **Render when settled.** Once every leaf is ✓, produce the branch's representation in the reference's form when one matches: the diagram, validated, or the prototype reconciled through mahou:prototype. The user asks for a different form when they want one, and when they want to compare, render the candidates side by side. When no reference matches, ask which form before rendering. The prose under the representation is the opening statement extended with the new leaves, not a new draft, and explains what the representation does not show. Numbered steps in prose refer to the diagram's numbers. When another note or an earlier branch already settles a behaviour, reference it in one sentence and do not draw it again; the representation shows only what this branch adds. Show the whole tree with the branch settled and stop. Open the next branch when the user approves.

### Types

| The branch is about | Reference |
|---|---|
| What is stored: new entities, fields, their shape and meaning | `references/types/data-model.md` |
| The shape of a structured value that a schema validates, not a table: a JSON column's content, a payload crossing systems, a tool's arguments, a step's config | `references/types/schema.md` |
| How a value moves between components: who produces it, who carries it, who persists it | `references/types/data-flow.md` |
| How a value is derived or a decision is made from an input | `references/types/rules.md` |
| The states one thing passes through, what moves it between them and what each state shows | `references/types/lifecycle.md` |
| Work the system does on its own after time passes: a scheduled job that picks records and acts on them, a wait that ends with the system acting | `references/types/scheduled-process.md` |
| What a program is made of: its components, what crosses between them, its inputs and outputs | `references/types/component-architecture.md` |
| What a component agrees with the rest of the system: its inputs and their sources, what it exposes, the value it hands on | `references/types/contract.md` |
| What the user sees on a screen: placement, states, encodings, interactions | `references/types/ui.md` |
| How the constructs of a source map to what a value carries: which part each becomes and in what form | `references/types/mapping.md` |

A branch that fits none of these is worked out with the user. A type that turns out to generalize beyond this session is a candidate for mahou:learn to add to this table.

## Recording

When the tree is complete, the project's docs record it, and mahou:write-documentation owns that. Before handing off:

1. **Existing notes the change touches.** Read every note in the docs folder before proposing the list, routing that reading through a `mahou:docs-scout` so it stays out of the conversation. List every note the change touches, not only the ones this session happened to open. A note belongs on the list when it describes the entity, the flow, the screens or the events the change alters, even when nothing in this session read it. Give each one what it would need, and say which notes you read and found untouched. The user settles each one: update it, add the minimum and point to the new note, or skip it.

2. **New notes.** The change may need one note or several. Propose the split, and the user settles it. Split by flow or part of the system, and keep everything about one flow or part in its note: its screens, its states, the client's local state for it and its rules. A branch about one concern across flows, such as the screens or the client's local state, has its content split into the notes of the flows it belongs to.

Then run mahou:write-documentation once, giving it the tree and every settled amendment, so the pass weighs the whole documentation rather than one note at a time. Each settled branch already carries its prose and its representation, so drafting is mostly moving that text into the note; `write-documentation` fits it to the project's charter and templates, which this skill never reads.

When the docs are written, check the scratch folder as mahou:basics says under Status.

## What this skill is not

It does not choose endpoints, functions, files or test cases, does not write code, does not commit, and does not write into the docs folder itself. When the user decides that a piece of the change goes straight into a repository, that is their decision and happens outside this skill.
